chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who ate suhur, then left his house, and the dawn had risen and become distinct, so he said:
"He completes his fast that day, then he must make it up; and if he ate suhur in a month other than Ramadan after the rising of dawn, he breaks his fast."

Then he said, "My father was praying one night while I was eating, so he finished and said, 'As for Ja'far, he has eaten and drunk after dawn.' So he ordered me, and I broke my fast that day in a month other than Ramadan."

Because he started with eating and drinking and did not look at the dawn, and whoever does that, his ruling is what we mentioned. Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And if he asked someone else about the dawn, and that person informed him that it had not risen, and he trusted him, so he ate and drank, then he learned that it had risen, then he must make it up.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting if one eats after dawn has risen but was unaware of it?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between *qada'* (making up the fast) and *kaffarah* (expiation) for unintentional eating after dawn, emphasizing that validity depends on whether the act occurred during Ramadan or outside it. Al-Sheikh al-Tusi adds a nuanced scholarly layer by addressing *taqlid* (following another's testimony), ruling that if one relies on another's report that dawn has not yet risen and eats, but later discovers dawn had actually risen, the fast is broken and requires *qada'*. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of excusing the *ghalit* (unintentional error) while maintaining the obligation to verify religious timings.
